title: Two Simple Techniques for Increasing Meaningful Interaction During In-Person PD
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. passes along two lightweight facilitation techniques for anyone leading in-person professional development, a conference session, or an extended staff meeting, sourced from retired Idaho educator Darlene Dyer's account of a keynote by leadership developer Lowell Applebaum. Both techniques are designed to shift participants from 'listening to reply' toward 'listening to understand,' a disposition Stuart argues produces more meaningful conversations and more constructive debate among adults. The first, 'Ask Me About…,' has participants write a personal conversation topic on a sticky note below their name tag so that networking starts from genuine curiosity rather than job titles. The second, 'Pick a Picture,' has participants share and discuss a photo from their own phone, which Stuart notes his own principals have used to open staff meetings. He frames both as simple, transferable tools for facilitators seeking stronger interpersonal connection at the start of a session, whether that session is for adults or, with adaptation, for students.
points: Both techniques target a specific disposition — listening to understand rather than listening to reply — that a facilitator can deliberately design into the structure of a session's icebreaker.
'Ask Me About…' replaces name-and-title small talk with a self-chosen personal topic on a sticky note, letting genuine curiosity (not job function) drive the first conversation.
'Pick a Picture' uses a photo already on a participant's phone as a low-prep conversation starter that builds interest and memory more effectively than generic icebreaker prompts.

Techniques designed for adult PD facilitation can often be adapted directly for classroom use, since the underlying skill (listening to understand) is the same one teachers want to cultivate in students.
quotes: At the keynote, Darlene heard from leadership developer Lowell Applebaum, whose session emphasized a dispositional skillset we'd like all of our students and colleagues to have: listening to understand v. listening to reply.

We all had name tags, but to increase our getting to know each other, he had us all put a sticky note below our names that read "Ask me about…" I filled in "Retirement." Then we were off meeting others with what they had written as opposed to just their names.

The speaker also had us… take out our cell phones and find a picture that we could talk about. Then the same routine. I used a photo I had taken last week of a bull moose and a cow standing in the river that runs behind my house.
This was fun and a great way to learn something about someone besides just their name and title; it created a stronger interest and memory.

My principals at Cedar Springs High School have done something like this to kick off our staff meetings. It certainly is an enjoyable way to break the ice or build connection at the start of a meeting.
